meta.home: I'm Lorenzo. I build software for the parts of a business that are still done by hand. Tell me what isn't working and we'll work out the rest.
meta.work: Five projects: a travel eSIM, software that watches camera feeds, a product of my own, an engine I published, and a course I wrote. What each one was, and what was hard about it.
meta.about: How I work, what I do before I write any code, and a bit about who I am.

hero.status: Open to a couple of projects
hero.lede: I'm Lorenzo. People come to me when something in the business is slow, gets done twice, or lives in a spreadsheet only one person really understands.

capabilities.title: What people come to me with.
capabilities.lede: One of these is usually close enough to yours to start from.

manualWork.title: Work your team still does by hand
manualWork.body: The report somebody rebuilds every Monday, or numbers copied out of one system and typed into another.

customTool.title: The tool you wish existed
customTool.body: The thing you do differently from everyone else, currently held together by three spreadsheets and one person's memory.

ideaToProduct.title: An idea that needs to become a product
ideaToProduct.body: You know what it should do, not yet what it looks like. I took my own product from exactly there to live.

systemsTalking.title: Tools that don't talk to each other
systemsTalking.body: Your accounting software, whatever the sales team lives in, a supplier's site. Moving information between them without anyone retyping it.

aiWhereItPays.title: AI where it actually saves time
aiWhereItPays.body: I've built it into a product people pay for and I teach a course on it. That's mostly how I know where it stops paying off.

outgrown.title: Something you've outgrown
outgrown.body: It still works, but every small change takes weeks and nobody wants to be the one who breaks it.

work.title: Five projects you can go and open.
work.lede: The day job, client work, a product of my own, an engine I published and a course.
work.pageTitle: Five projects, and the hard part of each.
work.pageLede: Not everything I've made. These five cover the most ground, and each one gets the full story.

course.formatValue: Online, recorded, at your own pace
course.lengthValue: Two modules, eleven lessons, about four weeks
course.note: The only thing here that isn't software. It's on the list because explaining something to people who will go and test it that same evening is a different skill from building it.

barcaMobile.summary: A travel eSIM sold under the FC Barcelona name. The product I work on day to day.
barcaMobile.situation: Barça Mobile sells mobile data in over 170 countries. The person buying it is usually standing in a terminal with no signal yet.
barcaMobile.contribution: Senior engineer on the team that builds it, across the app, the site and the parts behind both. Picking a destination, buying a plan, getting the eSIM onto the phone.
barcaMobile.challenge: Installing an eSIM happens once, on borrowed airport wifi, and if it goes wrong nobody tries again. Most of the care goes into the few screens that can fail quietly.
barcaMobile.proof: A real product with paying customers, release after release. Other people's code, and problems that surface long after you thought you were finished.

examin.summary: Software that watches camera feeds and tells people what just happened.
examin.situation: Plenty of businesses have cameras everywhere and nobody with time to watch them. Examin uses the cameras they already own, across jobs as different as solar farms and number plates.
examin.contribution: Brought in to build the product: live views, alerts, the evidence attached to each one, and the parts underneath keeping it connected to the cameras. There was no specification, so I helped decide what it should be.
examin.challenge: Restraint. An alert nobody trusts is worse than no alert, because people mute it inside a week. Most of the work went into what not to show.
examin.proof: Somebody handed me a complicated product and let me help decide what it should be. That's the shape of problem I'm used to.

ainterest.summary: My own product. Make images with AI, then put them somewhere other people can see them.
ainterest.situation: Every tool for making images with AI buries the results in a chat window. Whatever you made last week is gone, and you never see what anyone else is doing.
ainterest.contribution: Built the whole thing and it's live. Describe what you want, get an image, keep it in your account, publish it to a feed other people browse. Accounts, generation, the feed and the bill are mine.
ainterest.challenge: Almost none of the difficulty was the AI. One image is slow, costs real money every time, and sometimes fails. The app has to be honest about that without looking broken.
ainterest.proof: Someone had to decide what this was, what to leave out, and when it was good enough to show a stranger. Here that was me.

repolens.summary: Point it at a GitHub repository and it scores the codebase, with the file and line behind every point.
repolens.situation: Everyone has an opinion about whether a codebase is healthy. Almost nobody can show you where the opinion came from.
repolens.contribution: All of it, alone. Eight analyzers over the TypeScript AST, the import graph, the manifests, the lockfile and git history. A scoring model that shows its arithmetic, a Postgres queue, and the interface on top.
repolens.challenge: It reads code strangers wrote, so that code never runs: no install, no plugins, no scripts. The pipeline asserts exact findings against a fixture repo, so scoring can't drift.
repolens.proof: Most of the job in one project: analysis engine, queue, database, deployment, product. Every line is public, and the demo runs on a real open-source repo.

aiForFrontend.summary: An online course teaching developers to work with AI properly. I wrote it and I teach it.
aiForFrontend.situation: Developers picked up AI tools in a hurry and use them by feel. Some of it saves hours. Some of it quietly hands you something that looks right and isn't.
aiForFrontend.contribution: Wrote every example and recorded all of it. Two modules, eleven lessons: where these tools mislead you, how to ask for something usable, and how to use them on someone else's code, bugs and tests. Published by Itlogia.
aiForFrontend.challenge: These tools change every few months, so a course about the tools would date immediately. I taught the habits instead: what to check, what never to trust.
aiForFrontend.proof: You can't hide a vague explanation from people who will go and try it that evening. It's also where I drew the line I use when a client asks about AI.

builds.title: Nobody hired me to build these.
builds.lede: The businesses are invented, the software isn't. Book a table, buy a seat, or sign in to a console and work through three months of made-up invoices.

storefront.label: Guest side
storefront.title: Three hospitality sites, and the booking behind them.
storefront.lede: A beach club, a restaurant and a fourteen-seat counter, each with the admin screen the staff work from on the night.

console.label: Operator side
console.title: Two consoles for Monday morning.
console.lede: Sign in as an owner, an operations director or a single-site manager. Each role sees a different amount.

soleAndSalt.body: Loungers, a carta and ten nights in September. The free nights take an RSVP, so a guestlist fills up in the background and whoever works the door gets a screen.

casaMarisol.body: Reservations and online ordering on the same site, an order status page for after you've paid, guest reviews, and an admin the owner runs all of it from.

sundial.body: Fourteen seats and two seatings a night, sold as prepaid tickets with a QR code. A menu that changes with the season, a way to gift a seat, and a journal about the producers.

ledgerline.body: It reads the invoices and the closing notes overnight, then writes the morning brief. This one was entered twice. Avocados are 50% over their 30-day average. Every line links back to the record it came from.

tablevoice.body: Google, Yelp, OpenTable, TripAdvisor and the post-visit surveys land in one inbox. Replies come drafted in the group's voice, and the complaints that keep repeating get counted.

process.title: You talk to the person building it.
process.lede: No account manager, and nobody you've never met doing the actual work.

understand.title: Work out the real problem
understand.body: A conversation and a lot of questions about how the work actually happens now, before anyone decides what gets built.

scope.title: Agree the smallest useful version
scope.body: What gets built first, what it costs, and what we're leaving out on purpose. You get all of that in writing before any work starts.

build.title: Build it where you can see it
build.body: You get something you can click through long before it's finished, while changing your mind is still cheap.

handOver.title: Hand it over properly
handOver.body: It goes live and it's yours. The code, the accounts, and enough of a walkthrough that someone else could pick it up. I'm around afterwards if you want me.

aboutTeaser.title: One person, start to finish.
aboutTeaser.body1: I'm Lorenzo. During the week I work as a senior engineer on <barca>Barça Mobile</barca>, and I take on a small number of client projects alongside it. I'm also finishing a master's in computer science.
aboutTeaser.body2: I do every part of the build. The screens people click on, the services behind them, the databases, and getting the whole thing deployed. Which tools go into that is my job, not something you need an opinion about.

contact.title: Tell me what isn't working.
contact.lede: You don't need a document or a budget. A couple of sentences about what's going wrong is plenty. If I think it isn't worth building, I'll say so.

about.title: The longer version.
about.lede: How I work, how I decide what's worth building, and what I'm like to deal with.
about.intro: I'm Lorenzo. During the week I'm a senior engineer on <barca>Barça Mobile</barca>, and I'm finishing a master's in computer science.
about.freelance: Alongside that I take on a few client projects and keep my own products running, including RepoLens, an open-source engine that scores a codebase and shows where the score came from. That's where I try things out before they go anywhere near someone else's business.
about.career: Most of what I've built ended up in front of real people, and you find out within a day when something is confusing. I've looked after the parts nobody sees too, the ones that decide whether it still works at four on a Friday.
about.interests: The part I like most happens before any of that, sitting with a problem until it's clear what should exist. Most projects go wrong there, not in the code.
about.portraitAlt: Lorenzo sitting at a table on a terrace, with the Dubai skyline behind him.

principles.title: A few things I've settled on.

problem.title: The brief is a guess
problem.body: People ask for solutions, because that's easier than describing a problem. So the first thing I do is work backwards to what's actually wrong, then check that the thing you asked for would fix it.

maintainable.title: Someone has to live with this
maintainable.body: Whatever I build has to make sense to whoever looks at it next, and that might well be you. Clever solutions are usually just harder to fix later.

ai.title: AI is a tool, not a plan
ai.body: I use these tools every day and recorded a course on them. That's exactly why I'll say so when the answer to your problem isn't AI at all.

working.title: What working with me usually looks like.
working.intro: The things people tend to want to know before they get in touch.

noSpec.label: You don't have a plan
noSpec.body: Almost nobody arrives with one. Telling me what's slow, or what keeps going wrong, beats a document guessing at the answer.

notSure.label: Not sure it's software
notSure.body: Sometimes it isn't, and I'll tell you. Turning on a setting in software you already pay for is often the better answer.

tooSmall.label: It feels too small
tooSmall.body: A week of work that removes something your team does every day beats a six-month plan that never gets finished.

existing.label: Something already exists
existing.body: I can pick up what's there, finish something that stalled, or work alongside whoever built it. I'd rather not throw away what you've already paid for.

managing.label: You don't want to manage a developer
managing.body: You shouldn't have to. I ask when I genuinely need an answer, and you can see where things are without chasing me.

money.label: Cost and timing
money.body: You get a price and a date before any work starts. If either is going to move, you hear it from me while there's still time to do something.
